problem.title: On-device visual inspection
problem.context: A manufacturer inspects parts with cameras on 40 production lines across three plants. Each line has two to four cameras and an ARM edge computer with a small neural accelerator that cannot be replaced this year. Plant networks can be unavailable for days. Inspectors label about 5,000 defect images per week and models are retrained weekly. The team is two ML engineers and one half-time operations person, with a tight infrastructure budget.

requirements.text: Check every part as it passes the camera and signal a defective part to the line operator.
Retrain the model every week from the newly labelled images and roll the new model out to every line.
Collect the images the model was unsure about, or got wrong, so that inspectors can label them.
Each image is classified on the line within 200 ms, so the line never slows down.
When a plant's network is down for up to seven days, its lines keep inspecting with the model they have; the images collected in the meantime are uploaded when the network returns.
A new model reaches every connected line within 24 hours of approval. When a new model misbehaves on a line, the line operator can go back to the previous one within 15 minutes, without the ML team.
Cloud and infrastructure spending stays under 2,000 euros a month.
Three people build and run the system, with no support outside working hours.
The edge computers (an ARM processor with a small neural accelerator) cannot be replaced this year.

points.description: The system ingests data through messaging channels and runs ONNX-optimized, online inference in deployed edge modules, while orchestrated ML workflows handle preparation, training, tuning, offline evaluation, and deployment. Active learning selects uncertain or error-prone production inputs for labeling, scheduled retraining produces updates, and progressive release automation deploys them incrementally with rollback; retraining cadence may not respond immediately to detected changes.

The system packages model logic and runtime as a portable artifact, ingests data through messaging channels, and computes predictions online from current context and recent data. Human-reviewed labels support development, while retraining follows a schedule; workflow steps are manually script-driven, whereas release automation supports deployment and rollback with manual recovery intervention.

A managed cloud ML platform runs an orchestrated pipeline that ingests data through messaging channels, selects uncertain production examples for labeling, retrains models automatically, and evaluates candidates offline before release. The selected model is exposed as an online prediction service with elastic resources, while progressive deployment supports rollback if monitoring identifies quality or operational problems.

The system ingests data through messaging channels and serves current-context predictions online in deployed edge modules, using ONNX-optimized models for inference. Orchestrated, version-controlled ML workflows use active-learning samples, scheduled retraining, and offline evaluation before progressively releasing updated models with rollback; scheduled retraining may not immediately reflect rapid production changes.

The system ingests data through messaging channels and serves current-context predictions online in on-device edge modules, using ONNX optimization for runtime performance. Automated, orchestrated workflows support human labeling, scheduled retraining, offline evaluation, and progressive releases with rollback; scheduled retraining governs model updates while inference remains online.

The system ingests data through messaging channels and serves current-context predictions online on edge devices using ONNX-optimized models. An orchestrated pipeline spanning managed and pluggable engines selects samples for labeling, retrains models, evaluates candidates offline, and progressively releases approved updates with rollback if problems arise.

The system ingests data through messaging channels and serves current-context predictions online in edge modules using ONNX-optimized models. Automated, orchestrated lifecycle workflows use scheduled retraining and active-learning sample selection, evaluate candidates offline, track artifacts and deployment health comprehensively, and progressively release validated models with rollback support.

The system ingests data through messaging channels and uses orchestrated, automated ML workflows to label data with human review, train and offline-evaluate models, and version artifacts for reproducible deployment. Selected models are converted to ONNX and deployed for online inference on edge devices, while scheduled retraining and progressive release automation provide recurring updates with rollback if problems arise.

The system ingests data through messaging channels and runs orchestrated ML workflows across managed and pluggable engines, using active learning for labeling, scheduled retraining, offline evaluation, and version-controlled artifacts. Selected models are converted to ONNX and progressively released with rollback for online, on-device edge inference; scheduled retraining may not immediately respond to live quality changes.

approaches.idea: What if inference stays on the existing edge computers while a unified automated workflow handles labeling, weekly retraining, evaluation, and releases?
What if a portable and human-led workflow minimizes specialized MLOps infrastructure and operator burden?
What if a managed cloud platform owns training and online serving centrally?
approaches.dropped_because: Central online serving depends on network reachability and does not keep inspecting during a multi-day plant outage; it also fails to make the fixed edge computers the inference runtime.

approaches.idea: What if inference stays on the edge while training and lifecycle services use a hybrid, pluggable infrastructure with explicit artifact tracking?

trajectory.hypothesis: On-device ONNX inference should keep each line independent of plant connectivity and support Q1 and Q2. Active sampling and scheduled orchestrated retraining should serve R2 and R3; progressive rollback should help Q3, with the overall automation limited enough for C1.
trajectory.observation: The checked combination is compatible and has no adopting source. It supports edge inference, sampling, scheduled workflow, and rollback, but the values do not establish a 200 ms result, offline image buffering, or the requested deployment times.

trajectory.hypothesis: A portable package, manual scripts, and human review should reduce specialized infrastructure and labeling complexity for C1 and Q4, while scheduled training and recovery-oriented release support R2 and Q3.
trajectory.observation: The checked package and workflow combination leaves inference placement unsettled, so it does not ensure continued local inspection during network outages. Manual scripts also leave more recurring work with the small team.

trajectory.hypothesis: Managed cloud serving and elastic resources should simplify operation and automate weekly model production for R2 and C1, but may conflict with outage availability Q2 and the fixed edge constraint C2.
trajectory.observation: The point provides centralized automated training and releases, but online service placement depends on connectivity and leaves the non-replaceable line hardware unused. It misses key outage and hardware requirements.

trajectory.hypothesis: Adding artifact version control should make approved models and their dependencies easier to reproduce and roll back, strengthening Q3 and reducing manual recovery effort under C1.
trajectory.observation: Artifact version control reinforces release recovery, but does not itself guarantee device-side rollback speed or disconnected upload behavior. The point remains compatible and unattested as a whole.

trajectory.hypothesis: Moving inference onto the existing edge runtime, optimizing its model representation, and automating the workflow should fix B's outage weakness while retaining human-directed labeling and supporting R1, R2, Q1, Q2, and C1.
trajectory.observation: Edge inference makes inspection independent of central connectivity and reduces operational dependence on a live service. Human-in-the-loop labeling does not explicitly select uncertain examples, so it is weaker for R3 than active learning.

trajectory.hypothesis: Keeping inference local but using hybrid workflow infrastructure should preserve Q2 and C2 while enabling automated retraining and releases across connected plants for R2 and Q3.
trajectory.observation: Hybrid workflow infrastructure retains local inference and adds flexible engine choices, but its extra integration surface may increase operational burden. No source attests the complete combination.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replacing a basic artifact registry with comprehensive lifecycle traceability should improve training-to-deployment reproducibility and failure diagnosis, serving Q3 and C1 without disturbing edge operations.
trajectory.observation: The final point preserves the simple unified workflow and adds lineage across training and deployment. It still needs implementation-level latency, disconnected queue, cost, and rollback timing checks.

trajectory.hypothesis: Adding explicit artifact version control to the edge workflow should strengthen operator-accessible recovery and traceability for Q3 while retaining the lighter human review process.
trajectory.observation: Versioned artifacts improve reproducibility and support rollback, but this point still relies on inspectors to label examples without an explicit uncertainty-selection mechanism. It is weaker on R3 than the active-learning alternatives.

trajectory.hypothesis: Adding explicit artifact versioning to the hybrid lifecycle should strengthen model provenance and operator rollback while retaining the hybrid platform's flexibility.
trajectory.observation: The point combines edge inference, weekly scheduling, active sample selection, hybrid lifecycle infrastructure, and versioned deployment artifacts. It supports all functional requirements at the design level but its additional integration work may be difficult for the small operations team.

adrs.title: Where and how to serve line predictions
adrs.context: Every part must be classified quickly, inspection must continue during a plant network outage, and the existing ARM edge computers must remain in service. A centralized online dependency conflicts with outage operation; the design space does not establish hardware-specific latency.

options.name: ONNX-optimized edge inference
pros: Keeps per-part inference local to the production line.
Uses an optimization intended to improve runtime performance.
cons: Requires validation on the installed ARM accelerator.
Does not by itself guarantee the 200 ms target.
options.reason: Both retained alternatives need local inference for network independence; ONNX offers a performance-oriented deployment choice.

options.name: Central online model service
pros: Centralizes serving and can scale resources with demand.
cons: A network outage interrupts predictions and it does not use the fixed edge runtime.
options.reason: The cloud-serving seed missed the outage and fixed-hardware requirements.

adrs.title: How to collect examples and produce weekly models
adrs.context: The model must be retrained weekly from newly labeled images, including uncertain or incorrect cases, while sites can be disconnected and the team has limited operational capacity. The design space covers sample selection and workflow structure but does not specify durable edge buffering or synchronization behavior.

options.name: Orchestrated weekly active-learning workflow
pros: Connects weekly training, evaluation, and deployment stages.
Selects uncertain or error-prone examples for inspector labeling.
cons: Messaging-based ingestion does not prove seven-day edge buffering or reconnection upload.
options.reason: This best matches recurring retraining and uncertainty-focused labeling; offline evaluation precedes model promotion.

options.name: Manual scripts and human-directed labeling
pros: Keeps workflow structure simple and leaves labeling decisions with inspectors.
cons: Does not explicitly select uncertain samples and leaves recurring work with a small team.
options.reason: It is less suitable for explicit uncertain-image collection and weekly operation at 40 lines.

adrs.title: How to release models and recover from a bad update
adrs.context: Approved models must reach connected lines within 24 hours, and an operator must restore the prior version within 15 minutes without ML-team help. The space supports progressive release and rollback but does not specify these time bounds or operator controls.

options.name: Progressive release with rollback
pros: Introduces updates incrementally and supports restoring a previous model.
cons: The required rollout and rollback times still need concrete implementation mechanisms.
options.reason: It directly supports incremental deployment and rollback; both alternatives use it.

options.name: Recovery-oriented release with manual intervention
pros: Combines automated deployment and restoration with manual recovery intervention.
cons: Manual intervention is less aligned with operator-only recovery and the small team.
options.reason: The seed leaves too much recovery work dependent on manual intervention.

adrs.title: How to automate and source lifecycle infrastructure
adrs.context: A small team must operate training and releases. Unified automation reduces recurring manual work; hybrid infrastructure allows engine choice but risks greater integration effort. Neither alternative has measured monthly costs in the design space.

options.name: Unified automated lifecycle workflows
pros: Automates recurring workflow and operational activities without prescribing a large platform composition.
cons: Does not provide a cost estimate or prove the budget cap.
options.reason: The more direct lifecycle automation choice fits the team's limited operational capacity.

options.name: Hybrid multi-engine workflow infrastructure
pros: Allows workflow execution across managed and pluggable engines.
cons: Integration choices may increase setup and maintenance burden; cost is not established.
options.reason: This alternative accepts added integration work in exchange for infrastructure flexibility.

adrs.title: How much lifecycle lineage to retain for recovery
adrs.context: Operators need a reliable way to identify and restore a prior model, while the small team benefits from traceable training and deployment history. Comprehensive traceability offers broader diagnostic context; artifact version control is a narrower and simpler baseline.

options.name: Comprehensive lifecycle traceability
pros: Connects pipeline, artifact, run, metadata, and deployment-health information.
cons: Covers more lifecycle state than the immediate rollback need.
options.reason: This supports diagnosis across the full automated workflow.

options.name: Artifact version control
pros: Versions models and dependencies as managed assets for reproducible deployment and reuse.
cons: Provides less end-to-end context than comprehensive lifecycle traceability.
options.reason: The hybrid alternative retains a simpler artifact-level recovery baseline.

unaddressed.note: The space has runtime resource and infrastructure choices, but no alternative establishes total cloud and infrastructure spending below 2,000 euros per month. Estimate costs for the selected deployment before committing.
